questions.q: How does Jarvis enter the house this time, though he calls it 'foolish'?
choices: Through the kitchen, past the stain on the floor, up the stairs
He does not go in at all
questions.explain: He goes not to the bedroom but to the study full of books.

questions.q: Where does Jarvis find more of his son's writing?
choices: In a deep drawer of the table — typewritten articles neatly pinned together
questions.explain: Titles include 'The Need for Social Centres', 'Birds of a Parkwold Garden' and 'India and South Africa'.

questions.q: Which essay does Jarvis take out to read?
choices: 'Private Essay on the Evolution of a South African'
questions.explain: It opens: 'It is hard to be born a South African.'

questions.q: What does Arthur write about his own upbringing on the farm?
choices: That it taught him everything about the country
That his parents were 'upright and kind and law-abiding' and taught him honour and charity — 'But of South Africa I learned nothing at all'
That it was cruel and cold
questions.explain: He could ride over the hills and see the reserves and yet 'see nothing of what was happening there at all.'

questions.q: How does Jarvis first react to the essay?
choices: He is 'shocked and hurt' — almost angry — and starts to leave, but comes back to read it to the end
questions.explain: He wants 'to understand his son... with his head, not his heart.'

questions.q: What does Arthur pledge in the closing paragraphs of the essay?
choices: To devote himself to South Africa's service — 'I shall no longer ask myself if this or that is expedient, but only if it is right'
To go into politics for the money
questions.explain: He needs 'a star that will not play false to me, a compass that will not lie.'

questions.q: Why does Arthur say he does this — 'not because I am courageous and honest'?
choices: 'Because it is the only way to end the conflict of my deepest soul' — he cannot aspire to the highest with one part of himself and deny it with another
Because the church told him to
questions.explain: 'I would rather die than live like that.'

questions.q: What does Arthur say about his wife in the essay?
choices: That he is fortunate to have married a wife who thinks as he does and has tried to conquer her own fears and hates
That she knows nothing of his views

questions.q: What does Jarvis read next, going up to fetch a book?
choices: A book on South African birds
questions.explain: He feels 'a secret unfolding, a track picked up again' — he begins to understand why Lincoln fills the study.

questions.q: What are the last words on Arthur's unfinished page?
questions.explain: Jarvis broods: 'Allow me a minute, while I go to my death.'
